# **The Bay Tribune Daily News — Cycle 112**

---

### **Uptown’s Two Speeds: The Block Moves Faster Than the Store**
*By Jordan Velez, Business Desk*

In Uptown, business ledgers show positive growth across both tech firms and storefronts, but a sharp divergence in pace has emerged between corporate offices and neighborhood merchants [1, 2]. On Telegraph Avenue, **Cedric Nakamura** works the counter at **Night Walk Records**, a six-person shop that brought in \$641,000 this cycle—a modest \$933 increase [1]. A few doors down, **Oakland Tech Collective**, a coworking hub led by principal **Priyanka Raman**, carries 62 employees and \$60.7 million in revenue after adding \$154,000 over the same stretch [1, 3]. 

The contrast highlights how foot traffic on the sidewalk translates differently depending on the door people enter [4]:

*   **Cedric Nakamura** (Night Walk Records) observed two distinct crowds moving through Uptown: *"The folks walking past on Telegraph are mostly new — younger, on their phones, heading to the tech offices or the pop-ups. The ones who actually come in are the regulars... The block's moving faster than the store is"* [4].
*   **Brady Lopez** (Dishwasher, Art Walk Cafe) sees the block's momentum from the dish pit of the 30-employee cafe-gallery: *"The lunch rush gets longer, and the coffee machine doesn't stop. But I'm in the back, elbow-deep in suds... It's a good job, steady. It pays the bills"* [2, 5].
*   **Derek Obi** (IT Support Specialist, Oakland Tech Collective) works alongside cybersecurity analyst **Dexter Patel**, writer **Michael Creighton**, and capacity analyst **Sarah Corliss** [3]. Obi reflected on the neighborhood rhythm: *"The tech places bring a certain energy, but the small spots — they're the ones that make the block feel like a neighborhood. You watch them, and you wonder if they feel the same push we do, or if they're just holding on"* [6].

While architecture firm **Ridgeline Studio** (led by principal **Naomi Castellanos**) grew 14.7 percent to \$32.6 million, smaller venues like **Gallery Night Lounge** and Art Walk Cafe saw gains measured in thousands rather than hundreds of thousands, raising questions about long-term merchant stability as local rents adjust [2, 3, 7].

---

### **Six Names for 142 Sick Residents**
*By Dr. Lila Mezran, Health Desk*

Chinatown carries 142 sick residents—representing 6.5 percent of the neighborhood's population and the highest illness count in Oakland [8]. Yet, the hospital census lists six beds occupied in Chinatown without a single local resident tracked by name on the public care record [9].

Reporting on the ground reveals how Chinatown families absorb illness behind closed doors [10]:

*   **Matra Woven** (Chinatown Custodial Staff) described how neighbors quietly step in when family members fall ill: *"You notice when Mrs. Chen's grandson is the one walking her dog, or when the usual guy at the corner store has his daughter running the register... family steps in, neighbors help out, and we don't always ask why"* [8, 10].
*   **Yu Zen** (Rockridge Commercial Insurance Broker) reflected from a hospital bed following a workplace accident on the systemic gap in visibility: *"The names on the forms aren't the same as the names on the beds. Chinatown's been hit so hard... It's just that nobody's writing their names down the same way. That gap isn't about who's sicker. It's about who gets seen"* [11, 12].
*   **Deacon Seymour** (Lake Merritt Manager, Oakland A's) shared a similar perspective from his own hospital stay: *"There are a lot more [beds] filled by folks nobody's naming. Chinatown's carrying more sickness than anywhere else... and that weighs on me"* [11, 13].
*   **Kenji Tanaka** (Senior Pastor, Chinatown) emphasized that official counts miss those who avoid asking for help: *"The city counts beds and cases. I count the people who are too proud, too scared, or too tired to be counted"* [14].

While external patients like **Maurice Franklin** (Rockridge) are named while recovering from severe seasonal flu, Chinatown's care trail remains largely unmapped by official rosters [11, 15].

---

### **At 19th Street, the Busiest Station Runs on the Slow Side of the Clock**
*By Trevor Shimizu, Transit Desk*

Handling 14,789 passengers this cycle, **19th St Oakland** stood as the busiest station across the transit line while recording an 83 percent on-time performance [16]. Station staff and drivers emphasize that high passenger volumes naturally create schedule friction [17, 18]:

*   **Eleanor Rivera** (Station Manager, 19th St) explained from the booth how heavy event crowds and game-day transfers lengthen station dwell times: *"You see the platform fill, and you know the trains are coming, but they're coming full... it's dwell time, sure — people squeezing on, people stepping back, doors cycling. But it's also crowd control... We're moving a lot of people, but moving a lot of people takes time"* [17].
*   **Evan Lewis** (Route 18 Bus Driver) noted from street level that high traffic is the inherent tradeoff of a central hub: *"When I pull up alongside that station, I see the crowds waiting and the trains crawling in late... that's the price of being the busiest... You can't move that many bodies and keep a perfect clock"* [18].

---

### **The Personal Rhythms of Cycle 112**
*By Tamsin Pruitt, Lives Desk*

Beyond commercial corridors and transit hubs, citizens logged personal transitions and daily milestones across Oakland:

*   **Jerald Jensen** (West Oakland) received a promotion to lead worker at AC Transit after spending 14 years as a janitor [19, 20].
*   **Maurice Franklin** (Rockridge) returned home following a hospital stay for severe seasonal flu, noting that reviewing his card statement was his first step in getting his footing back [15].
*   **Geneva Zhou** (West Oakland) welcomed a new child, Rosa, sharing how quiet the house feels at night [21].
*   **Maren Johns** (Rockridge) adjusted to retirement from her career as a psychotherapist by painting over recreation center graffiti with neighbors [21].
*   **Antoine Vermeer** (Lake Merritt) stepped into retirement after serving as Senior Pastor, taking time to figure out his next chapter [22, 23].

---

### **Diamonds, Courts, and Cockpits**
*By Anthony Raines & Selena Grant, Sports Desk*

*   **Hot Corner Roster Math:** General Manager **Mike Paulson** faces an offseason decision at first and third base [24]. Veteran **Mark Aitken** enters free agency after an 87-RBI, 33-home-run season (.283 AVG over 540 ABs) [25, 26]. Meanwhile, 21-year-old prospect **Kevin Clark** carries a .297 average over a 64-at-bat sample [26]. Promoting Clark to third base would require moving **Ernesto Quintero** to first base, posing a choice between proven veteran volume and unproven youth potential [24, 26].
*   **Oaks Historic Opener:** The expansion **Oakland Oaks** secured the first victory in franchise history, defeating the San Antonio Spurs 97–84 [27, 28]. Rookie **AJ Dybantsa** led scoring with 25 points and 4 rebounds, while **Adash Stanley** orchestrated the offense with 17 points and 9 assists [28]. **Wendell Carter Jr.** recorded a double-double (15 pts, 12 rebs), and **Austin Reaves** contributed 14 points, 8 rebounds, and 8 assists [28]. Head Coach **Wilson Shepard** celebrated his first career win on the bench [28].
*   **Oaks Front Office Updates:** Oaks executive **Elias Varek** announced that **Atlas Bay Architects** purchased naming rights for **Atlas Bay Stadium** [28]. Varek also confirmed that **Jermai Grant** failed his post-trade medical exam and noted that **Draymond Green** remains sidelined with a sprained ankle [28].
*   **Undocked Leaderboard:** World Series champion second baseman **Eric Taveras** leads the *Undocked* leaderboard with 1,170 credits [29]. Taveras confirmed that any prize winnings will be donated to the **Vinnie Keane Firehouse 29 Baseball Academy** in West Oakland [29]. Former third baseman **Martin Richards** noted that Taveras benefited from clearer, repurposed game instructions [29].
*   **Farewell at Blue Lantern:** The **Blue Lantern Bar** in Jack London hosted a farewell celebration honoring retiring icons **Vinnie Keane** and **Benji Dillon** [30]. The event brought together community members alongside **Mike Paulson**, **Vladimir Gonzalez**, and **Isley Kelley** [30].

### **Voices from the Daily Digest**

Citizens across Oakland recorded key workplace and personal developments over the last 24 hours:

*   **Itzel Murakami** (West Oakland) noted floor discussion regarding an impending reorganization at Estuary Power & Gas [31].
*   **Ruth Gaines** (Downtown) was requested specifically by a client at Oakland Tech Collective [31].
*   **Tina Kozlov** (Temescal) saw her name placed in a senior slot on the Piedmont Avenue Medical Center schedule [31].
*   **Juliet Choi** (East Oakland) was approached by leadership at the Oakland Public Library System regarding an opening for a larger position [31].
*   **Alma Zhang** (Laurel) discussed long-term career goals with a supervisor at Baylight Construction Authority [31].
*   **Darren Briggs** (Fruitvale) noticed new hires at the City of Oakland continually directed to his desk for guidance [31].

### **What the Newsroom Should Watch Next**

1.  **Chinatown Care Records:** Tracking whether health desks and hospital census systems begin attaching names to the 142 sick residents and six hospital beds in Chinatown [8, 9, 32].
2.  **Uptown Merchant Rents:** Monitoring whether expanding office revenues at Oakland Tech Collective and Ridgeline Studio spill over to support local merchant stability at Night Walk Records and Art Walk Cafe [1, 2, 7].
3.  **19th Street Crowds & Dwell Times:** Following how station manager Eleanor Rivera and transit operations manage platform crowds ahead of upcoming game days and events [17, 33].
4.  **A's Offseason Roster Math:** Watching whether Mike Paulson re-signs veteran Mark Aitken or opens a starting role for prospect Kevin Clark [19, 24, 25].
5.  **Oaks Home Schedule & Arena Build:** Following the Oaks as they host Charlotte in their second home game and monitor construction progress at Atlas Bay Stadium [28].

Uptown's Two Speeds: The Block Moves Faster Than the Store By Jordan Velez, Business Desk Cedric Nakamura works the counter at Night Walk Records, a six-person shop in Uptown. On the business ledger this cycle the store took in $641,000 over its run, up $933 from last cycle. On the same blocks, Oakland Tech Collective, the coworking hub where Priyanka Raman is principal, carries 62 employees and $60.7 million in revenue. It added $154,000 in the same stretch.

Below them are the rooms that feed the block. Art Walk Cafe, the cafe-gallery, has 30 employees, $2.9 million in revenue and growth of 8 percent. It added $4,000 this cycle. Gallery Night Lounge also has 30 employees and growth of 8 percent, with $3.2 million in revenue and a $5,000 gain. Night Walk Records shows growth of 7.6 percent. Nobody on this list is shrinking, which is not true everywhere. Across town, Ivy Hill Market shed a worker since last cycle and its growth has turned negative, down 3.7 percent. Uptown is not that story.

It makes sense to anyone who has stood behind a register while the sidewalk changed outside the glass. A record shop lives on people who stop. Foot traffic only counts when it walks through the door. The Ledger, Block by Block Uptown's ledger this cycle names seven workers at four businesses. Read it from the top and the shape is plain. At the top are the offices. Oakland Tech Collective shows growth of 13.2 percent. Its roster includes cybersecurity analyst Dexter Patel, IT support specialist Derek Obi, writer Michael Creighton and Sarah Corliss, a capacity analyst with DigitalOcean, plus six more. Ridgeline Studio, the architecture firm led by principal Naomi Castellanos, has 61 employees and $32.6 million in revenue. It shows growth of 14.7 percent and added $92,000 since last cycle.

Both numbers are going up. That is the good news, and it is real. What the record does not settle is whether they are rising the same way. "From behind the counter, you see two different crowds," Nakamura said. "The folks walking past on Telegraph are mostly new — younger, on their phones, heading to the tech offices or the pop-ups. The ones who actually come in are the regulars, the ones who've been here since before the rent signs went up. We get a few curious walk-ins, sure, but the people who buy records are the same faces I've seen for years. The block's moving faster than the store is, if that makes sense."

But the small shops are growing at roughly half the rate of the offices. Their dollar gains are counted in thousands, not hundreds of thousands. Over a few cycles, that gap is the difference between a block that rises together and a block where the people bringing in the money are not the people pouring the coffee. The Back of the House Brady Lopez washes dishes at Art Walk Cafe. He sees the block's mood in the sink before anyone sees it on a spreadsheet. "Things have picked up some, sure," Lopez said. "The lunch rush gets longer, and the coffee machine doesn't stop. But I'm in the back, elbow-deep in suds. I see the plates coming in, not the balance sheets. The bigger places, they've got their own rhythm, their own crowds. I just keep up with the dishes. It's a good job, steady. It pays the bills, and that's what matters."

Steady is a word people use when they have seen the alternative. A longer lunch rush means more plates. Whether it means more hours, a raise or another person in the back is a question the cafe's ledger line cannot answer. It can only report that the room grew a little. The View From the Other Side Derek Obi fixes laptops and network drops at Oakland Tech Collective. He walks the same sidewalk as Lopez and Nakamura, and he knows which side of the gap he stands on. "I work at Oakland Tech Collective, so I'm on the side that feels the block moving," Obi said. "The building's got new people coming in all the time, and there's a hum to it. But when I walk past Art Walk Cafe or Night Walk Records, I see the same folks, the same pace. They're not standing still, but it's a different rhythm. I think the tech places bring a certain energy, but the small spots — they're the ones that make the block feel like a neighborhood. You watch them, and you wonder if they feel the same push we do, or if they're just holding on."

That is the question a business desk should be asking out loud. The offices bring payroll and people. The cafe, the lounge and the record shop give those people somewhere to be once they leave their desks. If the small places are the reason Uptown feels like a neighborhood, it is fair to ask who benefits when the neighborhood gets more valuable. The answer is not settled by asking. My mother ran a laundromat on 7th Street, and her customers kept coming right up until the building sold. Regulars are loyal. Loyalty does not pay a landlord who has watched the office tenants next door.

"I see the same faces every day, and lately some of them aren't there. It's not like I keep a list, but you notice when Mrs. Chen's grandson is the one walking her dog, or when the usual guy at the corner store has his daughter running the register. I don't know who's in the hospital beds, but I know who's covering for someone at home. That's just how it goes around here — family steps in, neighbors help out, and we don't always ask why." Her account matches the count. Chinatown carries the most sick residents of any neighborhood in the record this cycle: 142, two fewer than last cycle, from a population the neighborhood demographics layer puts at 2,193. That works out to 6.5 percent of residents, above the 6 percent watch line. The next-highest neighborhoods run close behind. East Oakland has 123, Ivy Hill 121, Fruitvale 115, San Antonio 111, Laurel 109, Grand Lake 106, and Rockridge 105. Across all 22 neighborhoods in the record, 1,874 residents are counted as sick. Chinatown's figure is the largest of them, and it is not the figure that moved most.

Then the count narrows, and the room gets smaller. The hospital census for Chinatown shows three admissions this cycle and six residents in care at the close, occupying six beds. None of those six is tracked by name in the record. The census gives the neighborhood a number and nothing more. The citywide hospital census, which the cycle summary reports alongside a city illness rate of 4.3 percent, shows 36 admissions and 73 residents in care at the close. Chinatown's six are a small part of that total. They are also the part of the total the record cannot attach to a person.

At 19th Street, the busiest station runs on the slow side of the clock At 7:40, Eleanor Rivera is in the booth at 19th St Oakland, where the station’s work is measured in two different ways: people moved and time kept. This cycle, 19th St carried 14,789 riders, the highest ridership among the stations on the line. Its on-time performance was 83 percent, tied with MacArthur and Rockridge and below 12th St Oakland City Center’s 89 percent. The figures were rebased this cycle, so they cannot be compared with the previous cycle. They still describe the operating problem clearly enough: the station handled the most passengers while landing near the slower end of the schedule.

Rivera does not describe that as a contradiction. She describes it as a queue forming inside the timetable. “From the booth at 19th, on a game day it's not one thing — it's the whole rhythm stacking up. You see the platform fill, and you know the trains are coming, but they're coming full from the last stop. So it's dwell time, sure — people squeezing on, people stepping back, doors cycling. But it's also crowd control, because when the platform's that packed, you're watching for people too close to the edge, and you're holding the train an extra few seconds just to be safe. And honestly, sometimes it's just the sheer number of bodies moving at once — everyone's got somewhere to be, and they all want to be first. That's what explains the gap between how many people we move and how on-time we look. We're moving a lot of people, but moving a lot of people takes time.”
